text: Complete Spring and Spring Boot Made Simple Every topic explained with a picture you will never forget + a working code example How to use these notes 1. Read the story - it is the picture that sticks. 2. Type the code in a project from start.spring.io. Never copy-paste. 3. Say the REMEMBER line out loud. 4. Next day, rebuild the example from memory. Before Spring, know these Java tools Classes and objects, interfaces, inheritance, collections (List, Map), generics, exceptions, streams and lambdas, and basic SQL. Install JDK 17 or newer, Maven and an IDE (IntelliJ IDEA or Eclipse STS). Code here uses jakarta imports (Spring Boot 3 and newer); always create new projects from start.spring.io to get the latest stable version.

Complete Spring and Spring Boot Made Simple - page 3 PART 1 - SPRING FRAMEWORK CORE 1. What are Spring and Spring Boot? Spring is a powerful Java framework that manages your objects and wires them together, like a building contractor who hires electricians, plumbers and painters so you only design the house. Spring Boot is Spring with everything pre-assembled: embedded server, automatic setup, no XML. Spring = engine parts. Spring Boot = the finished car, ready to drive. // The ENTIRE Spring Boot web app can be this small: @SpringBootApplication public class DemoApplication { public static void main(String[] args) { SpringApplication.run(DemoApplication.class, args); } } @RestController class HelloController { @GetMapping("/hello") String hello() { return "Hello, Spring Boot!"; // open http://localhost:8080/hello } } // Needs: Java 17+, Maven or Gradle. No Tomcat install, no XML. REMEMBER: Spring = manages objects. Spring Boot = Spring that starts with zero setup.

Complete Spring and Spring Boot Made Simple - page 4 2. Inversion of Control (IoC) and Dependency Injection (DI) Normally YOU create the objects you need (new). With IoC, Spring creates them and hands them to you. Restaurant story: you do not go into the kitchen and cook - the waiter brings the dish. A dependency is something a class needs (a chef needs a knife). Injection = Spring gives it, you don't build it. // WITHOUT Spring: tightly glued, hard to test or change class OrderService { private EmailService email = new EmailService(); // you create it } // WITH Spring: loosely coupled @Service class EmailService { void send(String to) { /* ... */ } } @Service class OrderService { private final EmailService email; OrderService(EmailService email) { // Spring injects it for you this.email = email; } void placeOrder() { email.send("customer@mail.com"); } } // Benefits: easy to swap implementations,

{ private final EmailService email; OrderService(EmailService email) { // Spring injects it for you this.email = email; } void placeOrder() { email.send("customer@mail.com"); } } // Benefits: easy to swap implementations, easy to test with fake objects. REMEMBER: IoC = Spring controls object creation. DI = Spring hands you what you need. 3. Beans and the Spring Container A bean is simply an object that Spring manages. The container (ApplicationContext) is the warehouse that creates, stores and delivers beans. Spring finds beans by scanning your code for special annotations (component scanning). @SpringBootApplication public class App { public static void main(String[] args) { // run() returns the container ApplicationContext ctx = SpringApplication.run(App.class, args); OrderService svc = ctx.getBean(OrderService.class); // ask for a bean svc.placeOrder(); System.out.println(ctx.getBeanDefinitionCount() + " beans loaded"); } } // Container types: BeanFactory (basic) -> ApplicationContext (full-featured). // In real code you rarely call getBean(); you just use dependency injection. REMEMBER:

svc.placeOrder(); System.out.println(ctx.getBeanDefinitionCount() + " beans loaded"); } } // Container types: BeanFactory (basic) -> ApplicationContext (full-featured). // In real code you rarely call getBean(); you just use dependency injection. REMEMBER: Bean = object managed by Spring. ApplicationContext = the bean warehouse.

Complete Spring and Spring Boot Made Simple - page 5 4. Creating Beans: @Component, @Service, @Repository, @Bean Stereotype annotations are name badges that tell Spring 'manage me'. They all work the same; the badge shows the role. Use @Bean inside a @Configuration class when you cannot annotate the class (third-party libraries). @Component class Helper { } // general-purpose bean @Service class UserService { } // business logic @Repository class UserDao { } // database access (adds exception translation) @Controller class PageController { } // web layer (returns views) @RestController class ApiController { } // web layer (returns JSON) // @Bean: you build the object, Spring manages it @Configuration class AppConfig { @Bean public ModelMapper modelMapper() { return new ModelMapper(); // library class, not ours } @Bean public PasswordEncoder passwordEncoder() { return new BCryptPasswordEncoder(); } } REMEMBER: @Component family = my classes. @Bean method = classes I cannot annotate.

Complete Spring and Spring Boot Made Simple - page 6 5. Types of Injection: Constructor, Setter, Field Three ways to receive a dependency. Constructor injection is the best: the object is never half-built, fields can be final, and tests are easy. Field injection hides dependencies and is discouraged. @Service class A { private final B b; A(B b) { this.b = b; } // 1. CONSTRUCTOR (recommended) // With ONE constructor, @Autowired is optional. } @Service class C { private B b; @Autowired void setB(B b) { this.b = b; } // 2. SETTER (optional dependencies) } @Service class D { @Autowired private B b; // 3. FIELD (avoid) } // Two beans of the same type? Tell Spring which one: interface Payment { } @Service @Primary class UpiPayment implements Payment { } // default choice @Service("card") class CardPayment implements Payment { } @Service class Checkout { Checkout(@Qualifier("card") Payment p)

one: interface Payment { } @Service @Primary class UpiPayment implements Payment { } // default choice @Service("card") class CardPayment implements Payment { } @Service class Checkout { Checkout(@Qualifier("card") Payment p) { } // choose by name } REMEMBER: Prefer constructor injection. @Primary = default, @Qualifier = pick by name.

Complete Spring and Spring Boot Made Simple - page 7 6. Bean Scopes Scope = how many copies Spring makes. singleton (default) = one shared copy for the whole app, like one school principal. prototype = a new copy every time asked, like handing each student a fresh notebook. Web scopes: request and session. @Component // default = singleton class Shared { } @Component @Scope("prototype") // new object on every injection/getBean class Fresh { } @Component @Scope(value = WebApplicationContext.SCOPE_REQUEST, proxyMode = ScopedProxyMode.TARGET_CLASS) class RequestInfo { } // one per HTTP request // Because singletons are shared by all users at once: // NEVER store user-specific data in fields of a singleton bean! // (Thread-safety trap: keep services stateless.) REMEMBER: Singleton = one shared bean (default). Keep singletons stateless. 7. Bean Lifecycle Beans have a life: born (constructor) -> wired (dependencies injected) -> init -> in use -> destroy. You can

= one shared bean (default). Keep singletons stateless. 7. Bean Lifecycle Beans have a life: born (constructor) -> wired (dependencies injected) -> init -> in use -> destroy. You can run code at the init and destroy moments. @Component public class CacheLoader { public CacheLoader() { System.out.println("1. Constructor"); } @PostConstruct // jakarta.annotation.PostConstruct void init() { System.out.println("2. Ready: load cache"); } @PreDestroy // jakarta.annotation.PreDestroy void cleanup() { System.out.println("3. Closing: free resources"); } } // Same idea with @Bean: // @Bean(initMethod = "start", destroyMethod = "stop") // Order: constructor -> dependency injection -> @PostConstruct // -> bean used -> @PreDestroy -> bean removed REMEMBER: Constructor, inject, @PostConstruct, use, @PreDestroy.

Complete Spring and Spring Boot Made Simple - page 8 8. Properties, @Value and Profiles Never hard-code settings. Put them in application.properties and read them. Profiles give different settings for dev, test and production, like switching clothes for different weather. # application.properties app.name=Student Portal app.max-users=100 server.port=8081 # application-dev.properties (used when profile = dev) spring.datasource.url=jdbc:h2:mem:devdb # application-prod.properties spring.datasource.url=jdbc:mysql://prod-host:3306/school // Reading values @Component class Info { @Value("${app.name}") private String name; @Value("${app.max-users:50}") private int max; // :50 = default value } // Group many values (better) @ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "app") record AppProps(String name, int maxUsers) { } // add @EnableConfigurationProperties // Activate a profile: spring.profiles.active=dev // A bean for one profile only: @Profile("dev") @Component class DevSeeder {} REMEMBER: @Value for one setting, @ConfigurationProperties for groups, profiles per environment.

Complete Spring and Spring Boot Made Simple - page 9 9. AOP: Aspect Oriented Programming Some jobs (logging, timing, security) are needed in many places. Instead of copy-pasting, write them once and have Spring wrap your methods, like a security guard at every door of a building. Terms: Aspect (the guard's duty), Advice (what to do), Pointcut (which doors). // dependency: spring-boot-starter-aop @Aspect @Component public class LoggingAspect { // Pointcut: every method in the service package @Before("execution(* com.example.service.*.*(..))") public void logBefore(JoinPoint jp) { System.out.println("Calling: " + jp.getSignature().getName()); } @Around("execution(* com.example.service.*.*(..))") public Object time(ProceedingJoinPoint pjp) throws Throwable { long start = System.currentTimeMillis(); Object result = pjp.proceed(); // run the real method System.out.println(pjp.getSignature() + " took " + (System.currentTimeMillis() - start) + " ms"); return result; } } // Advice types: @Before @After @AfterReturning @AfterThrowing @Around // @Transactional and Spring Security use AOP behind the scenes. REMEMBER: AOP = write cross-cutting code

" ms"); return result; } } // Advice types: @Before @After @AfterReturning @AfterThrowing @Around // @Transactional and Spring Security use AOP behind the scenes. REMEMBER: AOP = write cross-cutting code once, apply it to many methods.

Complete Spring and Spring Boot Made Simple - page 10 10. Application Events A school announcement: one part of the app shouts 'something happened!' and any interested part listens, without the two knowing each other. record UserRegistered(String email) { } // the event @Service class UserService { private final ApplicationEventPublisher publisher; UserService(ApplicationEventPublisher publisher) { this.publisher = publisher; } void register(String email) { // ... save user ... publisher.publishEvent(new UserRegistered(email)); // shout } } @Component class WelcomeEmailListener { @EventListener void on(UserRegistered e) { // listen System.out.println("Sending welcome mail to " + e.email()); } } // Add @Async to the listener to run it in the background. REMEMBER: publishEvent() shouts, @EventListener hears. Loose coupling. PART 2 - SPRING BOOT ESSENTIALS

Complete Spring and Spring Boot Made Simple - page 11 11. Creating a Spring Boot Project Go to start.spring.io (Spring Initializr), pick Maven/Gradle, Java 17+, add dependencies, download the zip, open in IntelliJ or Eclipse. Always use the latest stable Boot version offered there. demo/ +-- pom.xml dependencies and build (Maven) +-- src/main/java/com/example/demo/ | +-- DemoApplication.java main class with @SpringBootApplication | +-- controller/ service/ repository/ model/ +-- src/main/resources/ | +-- application.properties settings | +-- static/ templates/ web files +-- src/test/java/... tests // @SpringBootApplication = 3 annotations in one: // @Configuration this class can define beans // @EnableAutoConfiguration set things up automatically // @ComponentScan find my @Component classes in this package and below // Run: ./mvnw spring-boot:run or press Run in the IDE // Build: ./mvnw clean package -> target/demo-0.0.1-SNAPSHOT.jar // Start: java -jar target/demo-0.0.1-SNAPSHOT.jar REMEMBER: Keep the main class in the root package so scanning finds everything below.

Complete Spring and Spring Boot Made Simple - page 12 12. Starters and Auto-Configuration A starter is a combo meal: add one dependency and get everything related, with compatible versions. Auto-configuration is the waiter who sees the ingredients in your kitchen and prepares the dish for you. Add the web starter and Tomcat plus JSON converters appear automatically. <!-- pom.xml --> <dependencies> <dependency> <!-- REST APIs: Spring MVC + Tomcat + Jackson --> <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId> <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId> </dependency> <dependency> <!-- Database with JPA / Hibernate --> <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId> <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-data-jpa</artifactId> </dependency> <dependency> <!-- Login and security --> <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId> <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-security</artifactId> </dependency> <dependency> <!-- Input validation --> <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId> <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-validation</artifactId> </dependency> <dependency> <!-- Tests --> <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId> <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-test</artifactId> <scope>test</scope> </dependency> </dependencies> <!-- See what was auto-configured: debug=true in application.properties --> REMEMBER: Starter = one dependency, whole feature. Auto-config = Boot guesses the setup from the classpath.

Complete Spring and Spring Boot Made Simple - page 13 13. application.properties vs YAML Two formats for the same settings. YAML is tidier for nested values. # application.properties server.port=8080 spring.datasource.url=jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/school spring.datasource.username=root spring.datasource.password=${DB_PASSWORD} spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=update spring.jpa.show-sql=true # application.yml (same thing) server: port: 8080 spring: datasource: url: jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/school username: root password: ${DB_PASSWORD} # from an environment variable jpa: hibernate: ddl-auto: update show-sql: true # Priority (high to low): command line > environment variables # > application-{profile}.yml > application.yml # NEVER commit real passwords. Use environment variables or a secrets manager. REMEMBER: Same settings, two formats. Secrets come from environment variables.

Complete Spring and Spring Boot Made Simple - page 14 14. Actuator and DevTools DevTools restarts your app automatically when code changes (a self-refreshing kitchen). Actuator is the health dashboard of a car: health, metrics, environment, beans. <!-- pom.xml --> <dependency> <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId> <artifactId>spring-boot-devtools</artifactId> <scope>runtime</scope> <optional>true</optional> </dependency> <dependency> <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId> <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-actuator</artifactId> </dependency> # application.properties management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,info,metrics management.endpoint.health.show-details=always # Try in the browser: # /actuator/health -> {"status":"UP"} # /actuator/metrics -> list of metrics # /actuator/info -> app info # Never expose every endpoint publicly; secure them in production. REMEMBER: DevTools = auto-restart. Actuator = /actuator/health and friends. 15. Logging Use a logger instead of System.out.println. Levels from quiet to loud: ERROR, WARN, INFO, DEBUG, TRACE. Boot uses SLF4J + Logback automatically. @Service public class PaymentService { private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(PaymentService.class); void pay(int id) { log.info("Payment started for order {}", id); // {} placeholder try { // ... log.debug("Gateway responded OK"); }

PaymentService { private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(PaymentService.class); void pay(int id) { log.info("Payment started for order {}", id); // {} placeholder try { // ... log.debug("Gateway responded OK"); } catch (Exception e) { log.error("Payment failed for order {}", id, e); // prints stack trace } } } // With Lombok: @Slf4j on the class, then use log.info("...") # application.properties logging.level.root=INFO logging.level.com.example=DEBUG logging.level.org.hibernate.SQL=DEBUG logging.file.name=app.log REMEMBER: log.info("text {}", value). Never log passwords.

Complete Spring and Spring Boot Made Simple - page 15 PART 3 - BUILDING REST APIs WITH SPRING MVC 16. How a Web Request Travels (Spring MVC) Think of a restaurant: the DispatcherServlet is the receptionist who receives every guest, the HandlerMapping finds the right waiter (controller), the controller asks the kitchen (service), and the answer goes back converted to JSON. Browser / Postman | HTTP request: GET /api/students/5 v DispatcherServlet (front controller - the receptionist) | finds the right method via HandlerMapping v @RestController method (the waiter) | calls v @Service (business rules - the chef) | calls v @Repository / Database (the pantry) | v result object -> Jackson converts it to JSON HTTP response: 200 OK {"id":5,"name":"Asha"} // MVC = Model (data) + View (display) + Controller (traffic cop) // In REST APIs the "view" is just JSON. REMEMBER: One front door (DispatcherServlet) sends each request to

// MVC = Model (data) + View (display) + Controller (traffic cop) // In REST APIs the "view" is just JSON. REMEMBER: One front door (DispatcherServlet) sends each request to the right controller method.

Complete Spring and Spring Boot Made Simple - page 16 17. @RestController and HTTP Mappings A controller is the waiter who takes requests. Each HTTP verb has a meaning: GET read, POST create, PUT replace, PATCH partly update, DELETE remove. @RestController // = @Controller + @ResponseBody (returns JSON) @RequestMapping("/api/students") // base URL for the whole class public class StudentController { private final StudentService service; public StudentController(StudentService service) { this.service = service; } @GetMapping // GET /api/students public List<Student> all() { return service.findAll(); } @GetMapping("/{id}") // GET /api/students/5 public Student one(@PathVariable Long id) { return service.findById(id); } @PostMapping // POST /api/students public Student create(@RequestBody Student s) { return service.save(s); } @PutMapping("/{id}") // PUT /api/students/5 public Student update(@PathVariable Long id, @RequestBody Student s) { return service.update(id, s); } @DeleteMapping("/{id}") // DELETE /api/students/5 public void delete(@PathVariable Long id) { service.delete(id); } } REMEMBER: @RestController + @RequestMapping + @GetMapping/@PostMapping/@PutMapping/@DeleteMapping.

Complete Spring and Spring Boot Made Simple - page 17 18. Reading Input and ResponseEntity Data arrives in three places: the URL path (@PathVariable), the query string (@RequestParam), and the body (@RequestBody). ResponseEntity lets you control the status code and headers of the answer. // GET /api/students/5 -> @PathVariable // GET /api/students/search?name=Asha&page=1 -> @RequestParam // POST with JSON body -> @RequestBody // Header / cookie -> @RequestHeader / @CookieValue @GetMapping("/search") public List<Student> search(@RequestParam String name, @RequestParam(defaultValue = "0") int page) { return service.search(name, page); } @PostMapping public ResponseEntity<Student> create(@RequestBody Student s) { Student saved = service.save(s); URI location = URI.create("/api/students/" + saved.getId()); return ResponseEntity.created(location).body(saved); // 201 Created } @GetMapping("/{id}") public ResponseEntity<Student> one(@PathVariable Long id) { return service.find(id) .map(ResponseEntity::ok) // 200 .orElse(ResponseEntity.notFound().build()); // 404 } // Status codes: 200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content, 400 Bad Request, // 401 Unauthorized, 403 Forbidden, 404 Not Found, 500 Server Error REMEMBER: Path

.orElse(ResponseEntity.notFound().build()); // 404 } // Status codes: 200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content, 400 Bad Request, // 401 Unauthorized, 403 Forbidden, 404 Not Found, 500 Server Error REMEMBER: Path = which one. Query param = filter. Body = data. ResponseEntity = custom status.

Complete Spring and Spring Boot Made Simple - page 18 19. DTOs and Records Never send your database entity straight to the outside world. A DTO (Data Transfer Object) is a custom parcel: only the fields the client should see or send (hide passwords, avoid loops). Java records make DTOs one line. // Entity (database) has everything @Entity class User { Long id; String name; String email; String password; /*...*/ } // DTOs: what goes in and out record CreateUserRequest(String name, String email, String password) { } record UserResponse(Long id, String name, String email) { } // no password! @Service class UserService { UserResponse create(CreateUserRequest req) { User u = new User(); u.setName(req.name()); u.setEmail(req.email()); u.setPassword(encoder.encode(req.password())); User saved = repo.save(u); return new UserResponse(saved.getId(), saved.getName(), saved.getEmail()); } } // Tools to avoid manual copying: MapStruct or ModelMapper REMEMBER: Entity stays inside. DTOs cross the border. 20. Validation A security gate that checks

new UserResponse(saved.getId(), saved.getName(), saved.getEmail()); } } // Tools to avoid manual copying: MapStruct or ModelMapper REMEMBER: Entity stays inside. DTOs cross the border. 20. Validation A security gate that checks input before it enters. Add spring-boot-starter-validation, put rules on fields, and trigger them with @Valid. public record RegisterRequest( @NotBlank(message = "Name is required") String name, @Email(message = "Invalid email") @NotBlank String email, @Size(min = 8, message = "Password must be 8+ characters") String password, @Min(18) @Max(100) int age ) { } @PostMapping("/register") public UserResponse register(@Valid @RequestBody RegisterRequest req) { return service.create(req); // runs only if validation passes } // Failure -> Spring throws MethodArgumentNotValidException (400). // Other annotations: @NotNull @NotEmpty @Positive @Past @Future @Pattern(regexp="...") // Validate path/query params with @Validated on the class + @Min on the parameter. REMEMBER: Rules on fields + @Valid on the parameter = automatic 400 for bad input.

Complete Spring and Spring Boot Made Simple - page 19 21. Exception Handling Instead of ugly stack traces, return clean, consistent error messages. @RestControllerAdvice is one complaints desk that handles errors from every controller. public class ResourceNotFoundException extends RuntimeException { public ResourceNotFoundException(String msg) { super(msg); } } // In the service: // repo.findById(id).orElseThrow(() -> // new ResourceNotFoundException("Student " + id + " not found")); record ApiError(int status, String message, LocalDateTime time) { } @RestControllerAdvice public class GlobalExceptionHandler { @ExceptionHandler(ResourceNotFoundException.class) @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND) public ApiError notFound(ResourceNotFoundException ex) { return new ApiError(404, ex.getMessage(), LocalDateTime.now()); } @ExceptionHandler(MethodArgumentNotValidException.class) public ResponseEntity<Map<String, String>> invalid(MethodArgumentNotValidException ex) { Map<String, String> errors = new HashMap<>(); ex.getBindingResult().getFieldErrors() .forEach(f -> errors.put(f.getField(), f.getDefaultMessage())); return ResponseEntity.badRequest().body(errors); } @ExceptionHandler(Exception.class) // last safety net @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR) public ApiError other(Exception ex) { return new ApiError(500, "Something went wrong", LocalDateTime.now()); } } REMEMBER: Throw custom exceptions; one @RestControllerAdvice turns them into clean JSON.

Complete Spring and Spring Boot Made Simple - page 20 22. Layered Architecture Each layer has one job, like departments in a company. Calls go only downward. Controller -> handles HTTP only: read request, call service, return response | Service -> business rules, transactions, mapping (@Service, @Transactional) | Repository -> talks to the database (@Repository) | Database // Rules of thumb // 1. Controllers contain NO business logic and NO database code. // 2. Services never touch HttpServletRequest or ResponseEntity. // 3. Repositories contain only data access. // 4. Use interface + implementation for services if you expect many versions: interface PaymentService { void pay(Order o); } @Service class UpiPaymentService implements PaymentService { /*...*/ } // Package layout (by layer): controller / service / repository / model / dto / exception // or by feature (bigger apps): student/ course/ payment/ each with its own layers REMEMBER: Controller -> Service ->

controller / service / repository / model / dto / exception // or by feature (bigger apps): student/ course/ payment/ each with its own layers REMEMBER: Controller -> Service -> Repository. Each layer one job. 23. CORS and API Documentation (Swagger) CORS: browsers block a React app on one address from calling an API on another unless the API allows it - a guest list at the door. Swagger/OpenAPI auto-creates a test page for your API. // Allow your React app (localhost:5173) to call the API @Configuration public class WebConfig implements WebMvcConfigurer { @Override public void addCorsMappings(CorsRegistry registry) { registry.addMapping("/api/**") .allowedOrigins("http://localhost:5173") .allowedMethods("GET", "POST", "PUT", "DELETE") .allowedHeaders("*"); } } // Or on one controller: @CrossOrigin(origins = "http://localhost:5173") <!-- Swagger UI: add springdoc, then open /swagger-ui/index.html --> <dependency> <groupId>org.springdoc</groupId> <artifactId>springdoc-openapi-starter-webmvc-ui</artifactId> <version>(latest from springdoc.org)</version> </dependency> @Operation(summary = "Get a student by id") // optional descriptions @GetMapping("/{id}") public Student one(@PathVariable Long id) { /*...*/

springdoc, then open /swagger-ui/index.html --> <dependency> <groupId>org.springdoc</groupId> <artifactId>springdoc-openapi-starter-webmvc-ui</artifactId> <version>(latest from springdoc.org)</version> </dependency> @Operation(summary = "Get a student by id") // optional descriptions @GetMapping("/{id}") public Student one(@PathVariable Long id) { /*...*/ } REMEMBER: CORS = who may call my API. Swagger = free interactive docs.

Complete Spring and Spring Boot Made Simple - page 21 24. Calling Other APIs: RestClient and WebClient Your backend can also be a customer of other APIs. RestClient (modern, simple, blocking) replaces the old RestTemplate. WebClient is non-blocking (reactive). @Service public class WeatherClient { private final RestClient client = RestClient.builder() .baseUrl("https://api.example.com") .build(); public WeatherDto today(String city) { return client.get() .uri("/weather?city={city}", city) .retrieve() // throws on 4xx/5xx .body(WeatherDto.class); // JSON -> object } public void create(PostDto dto) { client.post().uri("/posts").body(dto).retrieve().toBodilessEntity(); } } record WeatherDto(String city, double temp) { } // Older code: RestTemplate.getForObject(url, WeatherDto.class) // Reactive: WebClient (spring-boot-starter-webflux) -> returns Mono / Flux // Declarative: @HttpExchange interfaces (Spring 6) or OpenFeign (Spring Cloud) REMEMBER: RestClient = easy outgoing HTTP calls. RestTemplate is the old way. PART 4 - DATABASES WITH SPRING DATA JPA

Complete Spring and Spring Boot Made Simple - page 22 25. JPA, Hibernate and Entities JPA is the rulebook, Hibernate is the worker who follows it. This is ORM: each table = a Java class, each row = an object. You write Java, Hibernate writes SQL. Boot 3+ uses the jakarta.persistence package. @Entity // this class is a table @Table(name = "students") public class Student { @Id // primary key @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY) // auto-increment private Long id; @Column(nullable = false, length = 50) private String name; @Column(unique = true) private String email; private int age; // column "age" automatically @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING) // store the text, not the number private Status status; @Transient // NOT stored in the database private String temp; protected Student() { } // JPA needs a no-arg constructor // getters and setters (or Lombok @Getter @Setter) } enum Status { ACTIVE, INACTIVE } REMEMBER: @Entity = table,

temp; protected Student() { } // JPA needs a no-arg constructor // getters and setters (or Lombok @Getter @Setter) } enum Status { ACTIVE, INACTIVE } REMEMBER: @Entity = table, @Id = primary key, fields = columns.

Complete Spring and Spring Boot Made Simple - page 23 26. Spring Data JPA Repositories Write an interface, get a full database toolkit - no implementation code. Spring writes it at startup, like ordering from a menu instead of cooking. public interface StudentRepository extends JpaRepository<Student, Long> { // Student = entity type, Long = type of the id } // Free methods: save, saveAll, findById, findAll, existsById, // count, deleteById, delete, flush ... @Service class StudentService { private final StudentRepository repo; StudentService(StudentRepository repo) { this.repo = repo; } Student create(Student s) { return repo.save(s); } // insert or update List<Student> all() { return repo.findAll(); } Student get(Long id) { return repo.findById(id) // Optional .orElseThrow(() -> new ResourceNotFoundException("Not found " + id)); } void remove(Long id) { repo.deleteById(id); } } # application.properties (MySQL example) # spring.datasource.url=jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/school # spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=update (none / validate in production!) REMEMBER: extends JpaRepository = ready-made CRUD.

Complete Spring and Spring Boot Made Simple - page 24 27. Derived Queries, @Query, Paging and Sorting Method names become queries (findBy + FieldName). For complex ones write your own with @Query. Paging stops you loading a million rows at once. public interface StudentRepository extends JpaRepository<Student, Long> { List<Student> findByName(String name); List<Student> findByAgeGreaterThan(int age); List<Student> findByNameContainingIgnoreCase(String part); Optional<Student> findByEmail(String email); List<Student> findByStatusAndAgeBetween(Status s, int from, int to); boolean existsByEmail(String email); long countByStatus(Status s); void deleteByStatus(Status s); // JPQL: uses class and field names, not table names @Query("SELECT s FROM Student s WHERE s.age > :age ORDER BY s.name") List<Student> olderThan(@Param("age") int age); // Native SQL @Query(value = "SELECT * FROM students WHERE email LIKE CONCAT('%', :d)", nativeQuery = true) List<Student> byDomain(@Param("d") String domain); @Modifying @Transactional @Query("UPDATE Student s SET s.status = :st WHERE s.age > :age") int updateStatus(@Param("st") Status st, @Param("age") int age); } // Paging + sorting Page<Student> page

byDomain(@Param("d") String domain); @Modifying @Transactional @Query("UPDATE Student s SET s.status = :st WHERE s.age > :age") int updateStatus(@Param("st") Status st, @Param("age") int age); } // Paging + sorting Page<Student> page = repo.findAll( PageRequest.of(0, 10, Sort.by("name").ascending())); // page 0, 10 rows page.getContent(); page.getTotalPages(); page.getTotalElements(); REMEMBER: findBy + Field = free query. Use Pageable for big tables.

Complete Spring and Spring Boot Made Simple - page 25 28. Entity Relationships Real data is connected. @ManyToOne: many students in ONE school. @OneToMany: one school has MANY students. @OneToOne: person-passport. @ManyToMany: students-courses (needs a join table). The side with @JoinColumn owns the foreign key. @Entity class School { @Id @GeneratedValue private Long id; private String name; @OneToMany(mappedBy = "school", cascade = CascadeType.ALL, orphanRemoval = true) private List<Student> students = new ArrayList<>(); } @Entity class Student { @Id @GeneratedValue private Long id; private String name; @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY) // owning side: has the foreign key @JoinColumn(name = "school_id") private School school; @ManyToMany @JoinTable(name = "student_course", joinColumns = @JoinColumn(name = "student_id"), inverseJoinColumns = @JoinColumn(name = "course_id")) private Set<Course> courses = new HashSet<>(); } // Tips // - Always set fetch = LAZY for collections and @ManyToOne // - Return DTOs, not entities, to avoid infinite JSON loops // (School -> students

HashSet<>(); } // Tips // - Always set fetch = LAZY for collections and @ManyToOne // - Return DTOs, not entities, to avoid infinite JSON loops // (School -> students -> school -> students ...) // - cascade = ALL: saving/deleting the parent also saves/deletes children REMEMBER: mappedBy = the other side owns it. Lazy by default, return DTOs.

Complete Spring and Spring Boot Made Simple - page 26 29. Transactions: @Transactional A bank transfer: money must leave account A AND reach account B - or neither happens. A transaction = all steps succeed together, or all are undone (rollback). ACID: Atomic, Consistent, Isolated, Durable. @Service public class BankService { private final AccountRepository repo; BankService(AccountRepository repo) { this.repo = repo; } @Transactional // all-or-nothing public void transfer(Long fromId, Long toId, double amount) { Account from = repo.findById(fromId).orElseThrow(); Account to = repo.findById(toId).orElseThrow(); from.setBalance(from.getBalance() - amount); if (from.getBalance() < 0) throw new IllegalStateException("Insufficient funds"); // ROLLBACK to.setBalance(to.getBalance() + amount); // no save() needed: managed entities are saved automatically at commit } @Transactional(readOnly = true) // faster for reads public List<Account> all() { return repo.findAll(); } } // Default: rolls back on RuntimeException (unchecked) only. // For checked exceptions: @Transactional(rollbackFor = Exception.class) // Gotcha: calling a @Transactional method from the SAME class

{ return repo.findAll(); } } // Default: rolls back on RuntimeException (unchecked) only. // For checked exceptions: @Transactional(rollbackFor = Exception.class) // Gotcha: calling a @Transactional method from the SAME class bypasses the proxy // and the transaction does NOT start. REMEMBER: @Transactional on the service method: any error undoes everything.

Complete Spring and Spring Boot Made Simple - page 27 30. Databases, Schema and Migrations For learning use H2 (in-memory, zero install). For real apps use MySQL/PostgreSQL. Don't let Hibernate change a production schema: use Flyway or Liquibase migrations (version control for your database). # H2 for practice (add dependency com.h2database:h2) spring.datasource.url=jdbc:h2:mem:testdb spring.h2.console.enabled=true # browse at /h2-console # ddl-auto options # create drop and rebuild every start (practice only) # create-drop also drop on shutdown # update add new columns/tables (dev only) # validate only check the schema matches (production) # none do nothing -- Flyway: src/main/resources/db/migration/V1__create_students.sql CREATE TABLE students ( id BIGINT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL, email VARCHAR(100) UNIQUE ); -- V2__add_age.sql ALTER TABLE students ADD COLUMN age INT; -- Flyway runs each file once, in version order, and records it. REMEMBER: H2 to learn, MySQL/Postgres to ship, Flyway to change the schema safely. 31. The

The N+1 Problem and Lazy Loading Loading 100 schools then asking for each one's students fires 1 + 100 queries, like going to the shop 100 times for one item each. Fix: fetch together in one trip. // BAD: 1 query for schools + N queries (one per school's students) List<School> schools = schoolRepo.findAll(); schools.forEach(s -> System.out.println(s.getStudents().size())); // FIX 1: JOIN FETCH @Query("SELECT s FROM School s JOIN FETCH s.students") List<School> findAllWithStudents(); // FIX 2: EntityGraph @EntityGraph(attributePaths = "students") List<School> findAll(); // FIX 3: return only what you need with a projection / DTO query @Query("SELECT new com.example.dto.SchoolCount(s.name, COUNT(st)) " + "FROM School s LEFT JOIN s.students st GROUP BY s.name") List<SchoolCount> counts(); // LazyInitializationException = you touched a lazy field

projection / DTO query @Query("SELECT new com.example.dto.SchoolCount(s.name, COUNT(st)) " + "FROM School s LEFT JOIN s.students st GROUP BY s.name") List<SchoolCount> counts(); // LazyInitializationException = you touched a lazy field after the // transaction closed. Fetch what you need inside the service. // See the SQL: spring.jpa.show-sql=true (and look for repeated queries) REMEMBER: See repeated SQL in logs? Use JOIN FETCH, @EntityGraph or DTO queries.

Complete Spring and Spring Boot Made Simple - page 28 PART 5 - SECURITY, TESTING AND PRODUCTION 32. Spring Security Basics Spring Security is the security guard of your app. Every request passes through a chain of filters (checkpoints). Two ideas: Authentication = who are you? (login). Authorization = what may you do? (roles). Just adding the starter locks everything. @Configuration @EnableWebSecurity @EnableMethodSecurity // allows @PreAuthorize public class SecurityConfig { @Bean SecurityFilterChain filterChain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception { http .csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable()) // OK for stateless token APIs .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth .requestMatchers("/api/auth/**", "/swagger-ui/**").permitAll() .requestMatchers(HttpMethod.GET, "/api/products/**").permitAll() .requestMatchers("/api/admin/**").hasRole("ADMIN") .anyRequest().authenticated()) .sessionManagement(s -> s.sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS)) .httpBasic(Customizer.withDefaults()); return http.build(); } @Bean PasswordEncoder passwordEncoder() { return new BCryptPasswordEncoder(); } } // Default login (no config): user = "user", password printed in the console. // Old WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter is gone - use SecurityFilterChain beans. REMEMBER: Authentication = who, Authorization = what. Define a SecurityFilterChain bean.

Complete Spring and Spring Boot Made Simple - page 29 33. Users from the Database: UserDetailsService Teach Spring Security how to find your users and check passwords (always stored hashed, never plain text). @Service public class MyUserDetailsService implements UserDetailsService { private final UserRepository repo; public MyUserDetailsService(UserRepository repo) { this.repo = repo; } @Override public UserDetails loadUserByUsername(String username) { AppUser u = repo.findByUsername(username) .orElseThrow(() -> new UsernameNotFoundException("No user " + username)); return User.withUsername(u.getUsername()) .password(u.getPassword()) // already BCrypt-hashed .roles(u.getRole()) // "USER" -> ROLE_USER .build(); } } // Registering a user: HASH the password before saving // user.setPassword(passwordEncoder.encode(rawPassword)); // Method-level security @PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')") public void deleteUser(Long id) { /* ... */ } // Who is logged in? // SecurityContextHolder.getContext().getAuthentication().getName() // or in a controller: public String me(Principal p) { return p.getName(); } REMEMBER: Hash with BCrypt. Spring calls loadUserByUsername to verify logins.

Complete Spring and Spring Boot Made Simple - page 30 34. JWT Authentication Flow A JWT is a wristband at a concert: you show your ticket once (login), receive a signed wristband (token), and show only that for every later entry. The server needs no session memory. Token = header.payload.signature. 1. POST /api/auth/login {username, password} 2. Server checks password -> creates a signed JWT -> returns {"token": "..."} 3. Client stores it and sends it on every request: Authorization: Bearer <token> 4. A filter reads the header, verifies the signature + expiry, sets the user 5. Controller runs. Invalid/expired token -> 401 Unauthorized // Creating / reading a token (jjwt library, 0.12.x API) @Service public class JwtService { private final SecretKey key = Keys.hmacShaKeyFor( "change-me-use-a-long-random-secret-at-least-32-bytes!".getBytes()); public String generate(String username) { return Jwts.builder() .subject(username) .issuedAt(new Date()) .expiration(new Date(System.currentTimeMillis() + 3600_000)) // 1 hour .signWith(key) .compact(); } public String username(String token) {

SecretKey key = Keys.hmacShaKeyFor( "change-me-use-a-long-random-secret-at-least-32-bytes!".getBytes()); public String generate(String username) { return Jwts.builder() .subject(username) .issuedAt(new Date()) .expiration(new Date(System.currentTimeMillis() + 3600_000)) // 1 hour .signWith(key) .compact(); } public String username(String token) { return Jwts.parser().verifyWith(key).build() .parseSignedClaims(token).getPayload().getSubject(); } } REMEMBER: Login once -> get token -> send Bearer token -> filter verifies it.

Complete Spring and Spring Boot Made Simple - page 31 35. JWT Filter The filter is the ticket checker at the gate: it runs once per request, reads the token and tells Spring Security who the user is. @Component public class JwtAuthFilter extends OncePerRequestFilter { private final JwtService jwt; private final UserDetailsService users; public JwtAuthFilter(JwtService jwt, UserDetailsService users) { this.jwt = jwt; this.users = users; } @Override protected void doFilterInternal(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse res, FilterChain chain) throws ServletException, IOException { String header = req.getHeader("Authorization"); if (header != null && header.startsWith("Bearer ")) { try { String username = jwt.username(header.substring(7)); UserDetails user = users.loadUserByUsername(username); var auth = new UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken( user, null, user.getAuthorities()); SecurityContextHolder.getContext().setAuthentication(auth); } catch (Exception e) { /* bad token: stay anonymous -> 401 later */ } } chain.doFilter(req, res); } } // Register it in SecurityConfig: // http.addFilterBefore(jwtAuthFilter, UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter.class); // Never put secrets in the token payload: it is encoded, NOT

-> 401 later */ } } chain.doFilter(req, res); } } // Register it in SecurityConfig: // http.addFilterBefore(jwtAuthFilter, UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter.class); // Never put secrets in the token payload: it is encoded, NOT encrypted. REMEMBER: Filter reads Bearer token -> sets Authentication -> request continues.

Complete Spring and Spring Boot Made Simple - page 32 36. Testing Spring Boot Apps Pyramid: many fast unit tests at the bottom, fewer slice tests, very few full-app tests at the top. JUnit 5 runs tests, Mockito creates fake dependencies, MockMvc calls controllers without a real server. // 1. UNIT test: no Spring, just Mockito (fastest) @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) class StudentServiceTest { @Mock StudentRepository repo; @InjectMocks StudentService service; @Test void findsStudent() { when(repo.findById(1L)).thenReturn(Optional.of(new Student("Asha"))); assertEquals("Asha", service.get(1L).getName()); verify(repo).findById(1L); } } // 2. CONTROLLER slice: only the web layer @WebMvcTest(StudentController.class) class StudentControllerTest { @Autowired MockMvc mvc; @MockitoBean StudentService service; // @MockBean in older Boot 3.x @Test void returnsOk() throws Exception { when(service.findAll()).thenReturn(List.of()); mvc.perform(get("/api/students")) .andExpect(status().isOk()) .andExpect(jsonPath("$.length()").value(0)); } } // 3. REPOSITORY slice: @DataJpaTest (in-memory DB, rolls back each test) // 4. FULL app: @SpringBootTest (slow - use sparingly) REMEMBER: Unit (Mockito) > @WebMvcTest > @DataJpaTest > @SpringBootTest.

Complete Spring and Spring Boot Made Simple - page 33 37. Caching Remember answers to slow or repeated questions, like writing the answer on a sticky note instead of recalculating. Enable once, then annotate methods. @SpringBootApplication @EnableCaching public class App { } @Service public class ProductService { @Cacheable(value = "products", key = "#id") // 1st call: runs method public Product get(Long id) { // later calls: from cache System.out.println("Hitting database..."); return repo.findById(id).orElseThrow(); } @CachePut(value = "products", key = "#p.id") // update the cache too public Product update(Product p) { return repo.save(p); } @CacheEvict(value = "products", key = "#id") // remove stale entry public void delete(Long id) { repo.deleteById(id); } } // Default cache = in memory. For many servers use Redis: // spring-boot-starter-data-redis + spring.cache.type=redis // Same-class calls skip the cache (proxy rule, like @Transactional). REMEMBER: @Cacheable reads, @CachePut updates, @CacheEvict removes.

Complete Spring and Spring Boot Made Simple - page 34 38. Scheduling and Async @Scheduled is an alarm clock for methods. @Async says 'do this in the background, don't make the user wait'. @SpringBootApplication @EnableScheduling @EnableAsync public class App { } @Component class Jobs { @Scheduled(fixedRate = 5000) // every 5 seconds void heartbeat() { System.out.println("alive"); } @Scheduled(cron = "0 0 9 * * MON-FRI") // 9:00 AM on weekdays void dailyReport() { /* send report */ } // cron = second minute hour day month weekday } @Service class MailService { @Async // runs in another thread public CompletableFuture<Void> sendWelcome(String to) { // slow work... return CompletableFuture.completedFuture(null); } } // Call @Async from ANOTHER bean (proxy rule). In multi-server setups use // ShedLock so a scheduled job runs only once. REMEMBER: @Scheduled = timed jobs, @Async = background work. Enable both first.

Complete Spring and Spring Boot Made Simple - page 35 39. Microservices and Spring Cloud A monolith is one big building. Microservices are a village of small independent houses (users, orders, payments), each with its own database, talking over HTTP or messages. Spring Cloud supplies the roads and signboards. +----------------+ Client -------> | API Gateway | single entry, routing, auth +-------+--------+ +--------------+---------------+ v v v user-service order-service payment-service (each: own DB) \_______ Eureka (service registry: who lives where) ______/ Config Server = central settings | Resilience4j = circuit breaker # Spring Cloud Gateway route spring.cloud.gateway.routes[0].id=orders spring.cloud.gateway.routes[0].uri=lb://ORDER-SERVICE # lb = via Eureka spring.cloud.gateway.routes[0].predicates[0]=Path=/orders/** // Call another service declaratively (OpenFeign) @FeignClient(name = "user-service") interface UserClient { @GetMapping("/users/{id}") UserDto get(@PathVariable Long id); } // Circuit breaker: stop calling a broken service, return a fallback @CircuitBreaker(name = "users", fallbackMethod = "fallback") UserDto load(Long id) { return userClient.get(id); } UserDto fallback(Long id, Throwable t) {

// Circuit breaker: stop calling a broken service, return a fallback @CircuitBreaker(name = "users", fallbackMethod = "fallback") UserDto load(Long id) { return userClient.get(id); } UserDto fallback(Long id, Throwable t) { return new UserDto(id, "unknown"); } // Start with a monolith. Split only when you truly need to. REMEMBER: Gateway + Eureka + Config + circuit breaker. Don't start with microservices.

Complete Spring and Spring Boot Made Simple - page 36 40. Messaging with Kafka (and RabbitMQ) Services talk through a post office instead of phoning each other. A producer posts a message to a topic; consumers collect it whenever ready. Fast, decoupled, survives a service being down. # application.properties spring.kafka.bootstrap-servers=localhost:9092 spring.kafka.consumer.group-id=email-group spring.kafka.consumer.auto-offset-reset=earliest // Producer @Service class OrderProducer { private final KafkaTemplate<String, String> kafka; OrderProducer(KafkaTemplate<String, String> kafka) { this.kafka = kafka; } void orderPlaced(String json) { kafka.send("orders", json); } // topic, message } // Consumer (another service) @Component class EmailConsumer { @KafkaListener(topics = "orders", groupId = "email-group") void handle(String message) { System.out.println("Send confirmation for: " + message); } } // RabbitMQ: @RabbitListener + RabbitTemplate (queues, good for task distribution). // Kafka: huge streams, replayable logs. REMEMBER: Producer sends to a topic, consumer listens. Services stay independent.
